title: auld lang syne
short: 'Old long since': days long past, old times; Henley and Henderson gloss it 'Old long ago'.
body: The phrase combines 'auld' (old), 'lang' (long) and 'syne' (since, ago), so it means literally 'old long since', the good old days. 'For auld lang syne' means 'for the sake of old times'. Burns wrote to Mrs Dunlop in December 1788 asking whether the Scots phrase was not 'exceedingly expressive'. In the song the phrase is a refrain and an object: the friends are asked not to forget either old acquaintance or old times.

title: Origin and printing
short: Burns sent the song to Mrs Dunlop in 1788 and to George Thomson in 1793, claiming he took it down from an old man's singing.
body: Burns told Thomson that this 'old song of the olden times' had never been printed or written down until he took it down from an old man's singing. Henley and Henderson suspect the claim was partly a modest device, since Burns had certainly reworked older material, though they allow that he may have heard a traditional fragment. The song was printed in James Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, vol. V (issued after Burns's death, 1796-97), no. 413, and in Thomson's Select Collection (1799), where it was joined to the tune now sung everywhere. How much is Burns's own remains disputed; critics often credit him especially with the childhood stanzas.

title: Earlier 'Old Long Syne' songs
short: Burns's song reworks earlier pieces: a broadside printed in James Watson's Choice Collection (1711) and a version by Allan Ramsay.
body: Watson's 'Old Long Syne', a love-song attributed variously to Sir Robert Ayton and to Francis Sempill, opens 'Should old acquaintance be forgot / And never thought upon'; Allan Ramsay wrote another love-song on the same opening; and anti-Union and Jacobite parodies used the tune. Henley and Henderson reprint these. Burns kept the opening question but turned the song from love to friendship and memory, and from formal English to intimate Scots.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

title: a cup o' kindness
short: A drink taken in friendship; the chorus turns remembrance into a toast.
body: The 'cup o' kindness' is a cup drunk to good will. In Scots the chorus is often sung 'my jo' (sweetheart, dear) in place of 'my dear'. 'Yet' means still, even now, after all the years. The chorus, sung after every stanza, is the part of the song nearly everyone knows; it turns the opening rhetorical question into an answer: old acquaintance will not be forgotten, because we will drink to it now.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh, 1896), vol. III, text and notes

title: be your pint stowp
short: You will pay for (stand) your own pint-tankard, and I for mine: each will buy his round.
body: A 'stowp' or stoup is a drinking vessel or tankard; to 'be' one's pint-stoup means to pay for it. The stanza is jovial and practical, grounding the sentiment in the shared drink. In the Thomson manuscript this stanza came last; in Johnson's printing and in Henley and Henderson's text it is second, as in the archive. The tone is that of a tavern reunion between old friends, each insisting on paying his share, and it keeps the song from sentimentality.

title: braes ... gowans
short: Hillsides; daisies. The friends ran about the slopes and picked daisies as children.
body: 'Braes' are hillsides or banks, 'pou'd' pulled or picked, and 'gowans' daisies (Bellis perennis). The childhood memory is the emotional heart of the song: two children together in the fields, set against the 'weary fit' of adult wandering. The plain verbs ('run about', 'pou'd') and the small, exact flower make the memory concrete. Gathering daisies is a child's pastime, and the stanza's pairing of past play with present weariness gives the song much of its emotional force. Many readers think this and the next stanza are most fully Burns's own.

title: mony a weary fit
short: Many a weary foot of travel; 'fit' is Scots for foot.
body: 'Fit' is the Scots form of 'foot', so the line means they have trudged many weary miles since. The stanza contrasts the free running of childhood with the burdened wandering of adulthood, separated by 'Sin' auld lang syne'. The word 'Sin'' (since) answers the 'syne' of the refrain, so the last line of each memory stanza measures the distance between then and now.

title: paidl'd in the burn ... till dine
short: Paddled in the stream from morning until dinner-time (midday).
body: A 'burn' is a stream or brook; 'dine' is dinner-time, the midday meal in rural Scotland. The image of children paddling all morning pairs with the next line's 'seas between us braid hae roar'd', broad seas that have roared between them since, a powerful contrast of the tiny stream with the oceans of emigration and separation. Henley and Henderson print the song with this stanza fourth, after the stanza on the braes, so the memories move from hillside to stream.

anchor: seas between us braid hae roar’d
title: seas between us braid
short: Broad seas have roared between us: the friends were separated by distance, perhaps by emigration.
body: 'Braid' means broad. The line is often read in the context of Scottish emigration, to the colonies and the Americas, which was common in Burns's day; the song's later popularity among Scots abroad owes something to it. The verb 'roar'd' makes the separation loud and violent beside the quiet 'paidl'd'. Whether or not Burns had a particular separation in mind, the line generalises the experience of friends divided by time and distance, which is why the song has served for leave-takings of every kind.

title: fere
short: Companion, comrade (from Old English gefera, fellow-traveller).
body: 'Fere' (also spelled 'fiere') is an old word for a companion or mate, from Old English gefera, 'one who travels with'. It is often mis-sung as 'my trusty friend'. The handshake that follows ('gie's a hand o' thine') gives the custom of linking hands while singing the last stanza. The word survives mainly in Scots verse and ballads, which adds to the song's antique, traditional feel. Its sense of a comrade on the road fits the stanzas about wandering and separation.

title: a right gude-willie waught
short: A hearty draught of good will; Henley and Henderson reject the common mis-division 'guid willie-waught'.
body: A 'waught' is a deep drink, a draught; 'gude-willie' means full of good will, so the phrase repeats the 'cup o' kindness' of the chorus. Henley and Henderson note that the accent of the popular tune encouraged singers to divide it wrongly as 'a richt guid willie-waught', inventing a non-existent 'willie-waught'. The final stanza thus ends the song in a shared, ceremonial drink.

anchor: For auld lang syne, my dear
title: The tune
short: Burns's words first went to an older air; the tune now sung was joined to them in Thomson's collection (1799).
body: Burns told Thomson that the old air was 'but mediocre'. The melody now universal is first documented with the words in Thomson's Select Collection of 1799 (it resembles an air in William Shield's overture to Rosina, 1782, though borrowing either way is thought unlikely); it has since become the song of farewells and of New Year's Eve across the English-speaking world.

title: Form and stanza order
short: Ballad stanzas in common measure (alternating four- and three-beat lines) with a chorus after each.
body: The verses alternate lines of four and three stresses, the common metre of Scottish and English ballads and hymns, which makes the song easy to sing in company. In the Thomson manuscript the 'pint stowp' stanza comes last; Johnson's order, followed here, places it second, so the song moves from greeting and drink, through childhood memory and separation, to the handshake and the final draught.
